Work: In science work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. Work equals force times distance, W = F x d, and is measured in joules (J), where 1 J = 1 N x 1 m. If the object does not move, no work is done, however hard you push. A force at a right angle to the motion, such as carrying a bag horizontally, does no work on the bag. Work done against gravity in lifting an object is its weight times the height.
Power: Power is the rate at which work is done, or energy is transferred: P = W / t. Its SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. A machine that does the same work in less time has more power. Rearranged, W = P x t and t = W / P. Larger units are the kilowatt (1000 W) and the kilowatt-hour used for electric bills. Power is not the same as force or energy.
Kinetic and Potential Energy: Energy is the ability to do work and is measured in joules. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, KE = 1/2 m v^2. It grows with the square of the speed, so doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times larger. Potential energy is stored energy. Gravitational potential energy depends on the height above a reference level, PE = m g h. Other forms include chemical energy in food and batteries, elastic energy in a stretched spring and thermal energy of moving particles.
Conservation of Energy: The law of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed; it only changes from one form to another or moves from one object to another. For a falling or swinging object without friction the total mechanical energy, KE + PE, stays constant: as height falls, potential energy turns into kinetic energy. In real situations friction changes some mechanical energy into thermal energy and sound, so the object cannot return to its original height, but the total energy is still the same.
Simple Machines and Efficiency: A machine makes work easier by changing the size or direction of a force. Simple machines are the lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge and screw. A machine cannot give out more work than is put in. The mechanical advantage is the output force divided by the input force: MA = load / effort. Efficiency is useful work out divided by work in, times 100 percent, and is always less than 100 percent in real machines because of friction. A ramp needs less force but a longer distance than lifting straight up.
